title: Inbox zero: What it is and how to actually get there
summary: Here's everything you need to know about the inbox zero approach, whether it's worth trying, and the specific tools and tricks that get you toward a manageable inbox.
body_markdown:
Confession time: I'm a chronic email avoider. If you've emailed me in the past few months, rest assured that I still haven't opened it. At some point, I realized I'd rather get slowly buried under an avalanche of Kohl's marketing emails and Amazon delivery updates than deal with my inbox like an adult.


But you don't have to share my fate. After all, email doesn't stop coming just because you're tired of dealing with it. And there are probably some important meeting invites (and decent coupons) buried in your email. I may be currently drowning in an inbox cesspool of my own making, but I also specialize in testing and writing about productivity and tech. I'm here to help you benefit from doing as I say, not as I do.


Here's everything you need to know about the inbox zero approach, whether it's worth trying, and the specific tools and tricks that get you toward a manageable inbox.

-

4 ways to get to inbox zero


## What is inbox zero?


Inbox zero is a system for managing email, coined by productivity writer[Merlin Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin_Mann) back in 2006 when Gmail was still new and smartphones barely existed. It's a simple idea, even if it's easier said than done: your inbox should be a temporary holding area instead of a permanent home for every message you've ever received.


Mann's original framework sorts every email into one of five actions:


-


Delete


-


Delegate


-


Respond


-


Defer


-


Do


You clear your inbox not by ignoring it (who would do that?) but by deciding what each message requires from you and moving it out accordingly.


For example, a newsletter you signed up for during a webinar six months ago gets deleted right away, along with the Google Docs notification that you already responded to. A report your manager wants reviewed by Friday gets[snoozed](https://zapier.com/blog/gmail-snooze/) (deferred) to Thursday morning. A question a teammate could answer better than you gets forwarded along (delegated). And now for the hard part: it's time to send a response to that client email you've been avoiding because you didn't want to deal with it. Tomorrow-you will thank you.


The goal is to process messages as they land, rather than letting three weeks of unreads pile up into something that takes a full afternoon to tackle. Some people run this triage process daily, while others treat it as a Friday afternoon reset.


The concept of "zero" is all about having a process for triaging your email as it comes in so that you have zero decisions left to make about what's sitting in your inbox. An email you archived after replying still exists; it's just out of your way.


## Is inbox zero actually good for productivity?


It depends on who you ask. In 2019, Taylor Lorenz argued in[The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2019/01/case-inbox-infinity/579673/) that inbox zero had become impossible for anyone with a full-time job and multiple inboxes, and she proposed "inbox infinity" instead: set an autoresponder, tell people you probably won't reply, and let the count climb.


Not everyone has that luxury. The late Zappos CEO[Tony Hsieh](https://yesterbox.wordpress.com/) called email "a never-ending treadmill," but plenty of jobs don't allow the treadmill to stop. If you're in sales, support, or running a small business, an autoresponder that says "I probably won't see this" is a good way to lose a customer.


So is keeping your inbox clear good for productivity? That depends on how replaceable your attention is. Rather than chasing a specific number of unread messages, aim for a system you can actually stick to, whether that system ends in zero or just keeps your inbox from monopolizing your day.


## 4 ways to get to inbox zero


If you've decided an empty inbox is worth chasing, here's how to get there. It mostly comes down to picking smarter tools and learning when to let software make the small decisions you don't need to be involved in at all.


### Use an email app built for how you actually work


Choosing the right[email app](https://zapier.com/blog/best-email-app/) is honestly half the battle. If you're still working from a Gmail browser tab (guilty) or with whatever email app came by default on your phone, you're doing inbox zero with one hand tied behind your back.


Take[Shortwave](https://www.shortwave.com/) , which has some of the more helpful AI I've seen in email apps. Ask it to "make a list of all the tasks in the website redesign thread," and it pulls that list together intelligently instead of summarizing the obvious. Tell it "schedule a meeting with John in 2 days at 6pm," and the meeting lands on your calendar painlessly.


[Superhuman](https://superhuman.com/mail) is another AI-first email app with built-in features that make it easier to never touch your mouse. Everything runs on keyboard shortcuts: hit Enter to reply, Ctrl+J to draft with AI, and semicolon to drop in a saved snippet you've already written for the tenth time this month. It has a steeper learning curve than Shortwave, but once the shortcuts become muscle memory, archiving and deleting start to feel more like reflexes than chores.


Neither app is going to inbox-zero your account by itself. But what they do is remove the friction that makes you avoid opening your email in the first place. The gap between a good email app and a mediocre one is basically the difference between an inbox that manages itself and one that manages you.


**Read more:**[The best AI email assistants](https://zapier.com/blog/best-ai-email-assistant/)


### Let AI and automation handle the busywork


A lot of what clutters your inbox doesn't need a human decision at all—like receipts, shipping notifications, and that newsletter you bookmarked three weeks ago and never opened. These are the kinds of decisions you can hand off entirely.


Start simple: set up a[Gmail filter](https://zapier.com/blog/gmail-filters/) that catches shipping confirmations and drops them straight into an "Orders" label, skipping your primary inbox altogether. Do the same for the newsletters you've stopped reading but haven't unsubscribed from yet (if you're like me, there are at least a dozen). That alone clears out a decent chunk of your inbox before you've opened the email app.


For anything that needs actual judgment,[Zapier](https://zapier.com/) is your friend. You could build a Zap that triggers for every new Gmail message. Then, add[AI by Zapier](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-by-zapier-guide/) as an agentic step and give it a job: read the email, decide if it needs a real response, then either draft a reply in your drafts folder for review, or archive the message if it's just noise. You don't touch any of it until the AI hands you something worth your attention.


Even if you aren't comfortable letting AI make executive decisions on what constitutes "noise" vs "vague and weirdly truncated message from your boss, sent from his iPhone, that he's still definitely expecting you to respond to ASAP," you can still have AI by Zapier sort your emails into folders and start drafting responses for anything it can. That way, you're coming to your email with at least half the work done for you.


**Read more:**[Email automation guide](https://zapier.com/blog/email-automation/)


### Manage your inbox from your AI chatbot


Instead of switching over to your email app to act on something, you can also get to inbox zero (or something close to it, anyway) straight from the chat window you're already living in.


Install[Zapier](https://zapier.com/blog/zapier-mcp-guide/) into a tool like ChatGPT, Claude, or Cursor, connect your Gmail account, and you've basically deputized your AI assistant to handle your inbox. Ask it to "summarize anything unread from the last 24 hours" before your first meeting, or "find every email in my inbox where someone's waiting on a yes or no from me." Tell it to "archive everything from LinkedIn notifications older than a week," and it just does it for you without you needing to build a Gmail filter from scratch.


One major upside is that your AI assistant isn't limited to email. Once it's connected to your inbox and, say, your[calendar](https://zapier.com/apps/google-calendar/integrations) or[Slack](http://zapier.com/apps/slack/integrations) , it can cross-reference all of it. That means it can catch the meeting request buried in an email thread and check it against your calendar in one go, giving you a clearer picture of your day and action items in one fell swoop.


[Try Zapier MCP](https://zapier.com/mcp)


### Just deal with it like a human being


You can use all the flashy tools you want (and as a tech obsessive who works at Zapier, I always recommend using as many fun tools as you can)—but sometimes the fix is simple. Just block off ten minutes each morning, coffee in hand, and run through your inbox with the delete/delegate/respond/defer/do framework. Set an actual timer, and stop when it goes off, even if you're not done.


You can even use the[Eisenhower matrix](https://zapier.com/blog/how-to-prioritize/) if it helps, sorting by what's urgent versus what's actually important, and sending the neither-urgent-nor-important stuff straight to the trash or unsubscribing.


Ten minutes won't feel like enough on some days (especially Mondays), but that's fine. Do it again tomorrow. They say the best way to eat an elephant is one bite at a time, and that admittedly disturbing metaphor has never been truer than when applied to a seemingly insurmountable task like taming your inbox.


## Pick a system, then actually use it


If most of your email doesn't need your brain, hand it to a few well-placed Gmail filters. If you're the type who needs one home base for everything, get a smarter email app and let it do the sorting. You'll probably also need to set aside a few minutes on a regular schedule to apply the delete/delegate/respond/defer/do framework to whatever is left.


Whatever system you land on, the fastest way to make it stick is to automate the parts that don't need your judgment in the first place.[Connect your inbox to the rest of your tools](https://zapier.com/apps/gmail/integrations) , and let the busywork handle itself.
